title: Observing the carbon-climate system
blurb: A progression from terrestrial carbon-cycle foundations through integrated towers, models, and satellite observations to monitoring and attribution.

person.name: David S. Schimel
person.affiliation: Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology
person.expertise: Terrestrial ecology, carbon-cycle science, ecosystem modeling, remote sensing, and Earth-system observation

papers.title: Terrestrial ecosystems and the carbon cycle

notes.takeaway: The terrestrial carbon budget combines large opposing exchanges, land-use emissions, and uncertain sinks driven by interacting biological processes.
notes.why: Begin with reservoirs, fluxes, and why an apparent missing sink is an inference with uncertainty.

papers.title: Recent patterns and mechanisms of carbon exchange by terrestrial ecosystems

notes.takeaway: Atmospheric and terrestrial evidence constrains regional carbon exchange, but attributing the sink to land use, regrowth, and environmental change remains difficult.
notes.why: A historical baseline for how multiple explanations can fit a global budget.

papers.title: A Global Terrestrial Monitoring Network Integrating Tower Fluxes, Flask Sampling, Ecosystem Modeling and EOS Satellite Data

notes.takeaway: A proposed monitoring network combines flux towers, atmospheric flask samples, ecosystem models, and satellite observations.
notes.why: See why no single measurement system can observe the entire carbon cycle.

papers.title: Terrestrial biogeochemical cycles: Global estimates with remote sensing

notes.takeaway: Remote sensing strategies must differ for photosynthetic exchange, land-use change, and the mechanisms producing additional ecosystem uptake.
notes.why: Schimel connects the quantity of interest to the observation required to estimate it.

papers.title: Observing terrestrial ecosystems and the carbon cycle from space

notes.takeaway: Remote and in situ observations together can reduce spatial sampling gaps in carbon stocks, fluxes, and plant traits, especially in tropical and northern ecosystems.
notes.why: Move beyond greenness indices toward ecosystem structure and function.

papers.title: Remote sensing of the terrestrial carbon cycle: A review of advances over 50 years

notes.takeaway: Five decades of work connect optical, thermal, microwave, lidar, fluorescence, and inversion methods to carbon stocks and fluxes.
notes.why: Use this review to compare what each observing approach measures and how its estimates are validated.

papers.title: Effect of increasing CO2 on the terrestrial carbon cycle

notes.takeaway: An analysis combining tropical and extratropical flux constraints finds a substantial CO2-driven contribution to land uptake, while emphasizing remaining uncertainty.
notes.why: Separate evidence for fertilization from assumptions about the persistence of that sink under warming and deforestation.

papers.title: The influence of rising tropospheric carbon dioxide and ozone on plant productivity

notes.takeaway: Long-term enrichment experiments reveal interacting effects of CO2, ozone, temperature, water, and nutrients on plant productivity.
notes.why: Use manipulative experiments to challenge mechanisms inferred from global observations.

notes.takeaway: This preprint argues for higher-resolution observations that distinguish heterogeneous carbon sources and sinks and attribute their changes to mechanisms.
notes.why: Read it as an observing-system proposal, then compare its ambitions with later budget assessments.

papers.title: Carbon sequestration and biodiversity co-benefits of preserving forests in the western United States

notes.takeaway: Scenario-based ecosystem modeling combines carbon sequestration potential, drought and fire vulnerability, and biodiversity in forest-preservation priorities.
notes.why: Connect carbon science to decisions while retaining scenario dependence and multiple ecological criteria.

papers.title: New views on changing Arctic vegetation

notes.takeaway: This perspective explains why long, consistent, spatially resolved records are needed to test interpretations of Arctic vegetation change.
notes.why: A continuing methodological challenge: distinguish a measured greening trend from its ecological cause.

notes.takeaway: Global Carbon Budget 2024 combines emissions inventories, observations, models, and inversions while documenting persistent disagreements in regional fluxes.
notes.why: The 2025 publication shows how budget closure can coexist with important uncertainty about sources and sinks.

papers.title: The Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation: High-resolution laser ranging of the Earth’s forests and topography

notes.takeaway: GEDI uses spaceborne laser ranging to measure forest vertical structure, supporting estimates of biomass and studies of habitat and ecosystem processes.
notes.why: Connect the episode’s discussion of three-dimensional vegetation observations to the instrument and its measurement requirements.

sections.label: Foundations: stocks, fluxes, ecosystems
sections.summary: Carbon science begins by distinguishing stocks from fluxes and by explaining how vegetation, soils, climate, and disturbance interact. These mechanisms define what an observing system must measure.

sections.label: Observation: towers, atmosphere, satellites
sections.summary: The field then combines tower fluxes, flask samples, ecosystem models, and satellite observations. Each observes a different projection of the carbon system, so integration is the scientific task.

sections.label: Assimilation: from measurements to estimates
sections.summary: Inverse and ecosystem models use heterogeneous observations to estimate sources and sinks. Their results remain conditional on transport, priors, calibration, and the structure of the model.

sections.label: Frontier: monitoring a changing planet
sections.summary: Current work asks whether carbon loss and climate stress can be detected early enough to matter. That requires provenance, uncertainty, and measurements that remain comparable as sensors and pipelines change.
questions: How fast can anomalies be attributed?
